questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the colonial grievance that drove Spanish American independence

stimulus.body: A colonial administrative record from a Spanish American province lists the offices held by peninsular-born officials, notes that local creole merchants supplied the transport and credit for the export trade, and records that appeals to Madrid about local offices had gone unanswered for years.

questions.stem: In tonight's revision session, your group works through why Spanish American independence broke from imperial rule.

options.text: Local creoles resented being governed by peninsular officials while excluded from the highest posts
The provinces suffered because the crown forbade the export of local goods entirely
options.misconception: invents a ban on exports that drove revolt

options.text: Independence was caused by a foreign invasion that ended Spanish rule in the region
options.misconception: attributes independence to foreign invasion

options.text: The creoles had no economic grievance, since the crown taxed all colonists equally
options.misconception: claims taxation was equal across the empire

questions.explanation: Creoles had local wealth yet were barred from the top offices and ruled from Madrid, feeding the grievances independence drew on. The record shows no export ban or invasion.
questions.hint: Ask who held the highest offices locally.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why creole discontent persisted in the Spanish empire
questions.stem: Your study group opens revision by asking what made creole discontent in the Spanish empire so persistent.

options.text: The discontent came from a collapse in silver output that ruined every creole household
options.misconception: blames a silver collapse for every creole grievance

options.text: Wealthy local-born elites were excluded from the top offices, so success fed resentment
Creoles were taxed at lower rates than other colonists, so they wanted more tax relief
options.misconception: reverses the direction of colonial tax burdens

options.text: Most creoles had never received any education, so they lacked the language of politics
options.misconception: claims creoles were wholly uneducated

questions.explanation: Creole elites could prosper yet never hold the top posts, which kept peninsular authority in place and fed resentment. A silver collapse, reversed tax burdens and widespread ignorance all misread this.
questions.hint: Ask who could rise but not govern.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why Brazilian independence followed a different path

options.text: Brazil was already independent, since the Portuguese court had moved to Brazil in 1808
options.misconception: treats the royal transfer as independence achieved

options.text: Brazil kept slavery longer, so its independence was purely a commercial decision
options.misconception: reduces Brazilian independence to an economic calculation

options.text: The Brazilian movement was smaller, so it had less influence on the wider region
options.misconception: claims movement size explains the difference

options.text: The Portuguese monarchy stayed in Brazil, so the struggle was against the court at home

questions.explanation: With the court in Brazil after 1808, elites fought the monarchy's rule in Rio rather than a colonial governor in Madrid, which shaped a different path. The other readings misattribute the difference.
questions.hint: Ask who was actually being obeyed in Rio.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Define nationalism from an example of nationalist rhetoric

stimulus.body: A printed slogan from a provincial crowd in the 1820s calls for the people of the province to decide their own affairs and to throw off rule from a foreign capital, and it names a language and a church as belonging to the people.

questions.stem: Before the session ends, the group defines nationalism by working from a printed slogan.

options.text: Nationalism is the defence of ancient feudal privileges against modern government
options.misconception: defines nationalism as defence of old feudal rights

options.text: Nationalism is a foreign policy of empire that spreads a ruler's authority abroad
options.misconception: confuses nationalism with imperial expansion

options.text: Nationalism is the identification of a people with their own political community
Nationalism is the rejection of all shared institutions between different peoples
options.misconception: makes nationalism a refusal of any shared institution

questions.explanation: The slogan ties a people to a language, a faith and the right to govern themselves, which is the core of nationalist thought. Feudal rights, imperial expansion and refusing shared life invert it.
questions.hint: Ask who the people are claimed to be.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how nationalism could unite and divide at the same time
questions.stem: Revision notes in your folder explain how nationalism could unite a people and also divide them.

options.text: Nationalism always unified a people, since every shared identity produced lasting agreement
options.misconception: assumes nationalism produced permanent agreement

options.text: It built loyalty to a common people, but the same claim sharpened conflict with outsiders
Nationalism divided only within cities, while national unity was complete in the countryside
options.misconception: localises disunity to the cities

options.text: Nationalism had no political effect, since it changed culture but never governments
options.misconception: denies nationalism any political effect

questions.explanation: The same appeal that rallied a people against outside rule could set citizens against each other, so nationalism built and broke solidarity at once. Permanent agreement, city-only division and no political effect all fail.
questions.hint: Ask who counts as inside the nation.
